hints: Think about what benzene loses and what $\text{Br}_{2}$ provides when $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{Br}$ forms, remember the benzene ring keeps its aromaticity so one H must go somewhere.
walkthrough:
Balance atoms around the substitution**
Picture $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6} + \text{Br}_{2} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{Br} + \text{?}$. Benzene swaps one H for one Br, so the displaced H and the second Br from $\text{Br}_{2}$ must combine. That gives $\text{HBr}$ as the only other product.

hints: Recall that the pi electrons of benzene act as a nucleophile toward the strong electrophile $\text{Br}^{+}$, so consider where the first curly arrow starts and ends.
Think about what the temporary loss of aromaticity looks like, with a positive charge delocalised in the ring and Br attached, and how a C-H bond then breaks to restore it.
walkthrough:
Let the ring attack the electrophile**
Think of benzene as electron rich because of its delocalised pi cloud. Draw a curly arrow starting in the middle of the ring (the pi system) and pointing to $\text{Br}^{+}$. This forms a new $\text{C-Br}$ bond. $\text{Br}^{+}$ needs no arrow from itself, it accepts the pair.

Draw the Wheland intermediate correctly**
Once Br attaches, aromaticity is temporarily broken. You now have a cyclohexadienyl cation: a six membered ring with Br attached to one carbon, two double bonds remaining, and a positive charge delocalised over the ring. Show the + inside or delocalised with a horseshoe. This is the intermediate in the middle box.

Restore aromaticity by losing H+**
The ring desperately wants its stable aromatic sextet back. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond on the same carbon that carries Br, back into the ring to reform the pi system. The H leaves as $\text{H}^{+}$, giving $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{Br} + \text{H}^{+}$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system to $\text{Br}^{+}$ to form C-Br bond; intermediate is arenium ion $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6}\text{Br}^{+}$ with Br attached and positive charge delocalised in ring (horseshoe with +). Then curly arrow from C-H bond to reform aromatic pi system, releasing $\text{H}^{+}$.

hints: Focus on the attacking species $\text{Br}^{+}$ and on whether H is replaced or added to the ring without destroying aromaticity permanently.
walkthrough:
Put the two clues together**
The attacker $\text{Br}^{+}$ is positively charged and electron loving, so it is an electrophile. Overall a ring H is swapped for Br and aromaticity is retained, so it is substitution, not addition. Together this is electrophilic substitution.

hints: Look at the change from benzene to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, identify which alkyl group has been added and what type of haloalkane could supply it.
Recall the Lewis acid catalyst needed to generate a carbocation-like electrophile from a haloalkane for attack on benzene.
walkthrough:
Spot the alkylation**
Benzene becomes ethylbenzene, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. That is addition of a $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ group in place of H, the classic Friedel-Crafts alkylation.

Choose reagent and catalyst**
You need an ethyl halide to provide the ethyl electrophile, so $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ (or Br or I version) works well. You also need a strong Lewis acid to polarise the $\text{C-X}$ bond, typically anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ ( $\text{FeCl}_{3}$ is also accepted).

Final answer: reagent: chloroethane / bromoethane / iodoethane, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ / $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$ / $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{I}$
catalyst: $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ / $\text{FeCl}_{3}$ / $\text{FeBr}_{3}$

hints: Remember what hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ does to any alkyl side chain on benzene, however long it is, and what product step 3 then reduces to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.
walkthrough:
Follow the oxidation then reduction logic**
Hot $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ with $\text{OH}^{-}(\text{aq})$ is vigorous oxidation. Any alkyl side chain on benzene, here $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, is chopped right back to a $\text{COOH}$ group attached directly to the ring. So A is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH}$, benzoic acid (isolated as benzoate then acidified). This fits because step 3 reduces the acid to the primary alcohol $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.
Final answer: A is benzoic acid, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH}$ (benzene ring with $\text{COOH}$ substituent)

hints: For step 3, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH}$ to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, think about which powerful hydride donor reduces acids but leaves the benzene ring untouched.
For step 4, phenyl to cyclohexyl conversion needs addition of hydrogen across three double bonds, consider which metal plus hydrogen gas does ring hydrogenation under pressure and heat.
walkthrough:
Reduce the acid without touching the ring**
Step 3 is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. That is carboxylic acid to primary alcohol. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is too gentle for acids, you need the stronger reducing agent lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ in dry ether followed by acid work up.

Hydrogenate the aromatic ring**
Step 4 is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{11}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. The $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ stays the same, the benzene ring becomes cyclohexane by addition of $3\text{H}_{2}$. This needs catalytic hydrogenation with $\text{H}_{2}$ and Pt (high pressure and heat), which forces the stable aromatic system to saturate.

Final answer: step 3: $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$
step 4: $\text{H}_{2}$ with Pt catalyst (Ni also used for ring hydrogenation, Pt specified here)

hints: Sketch $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{11}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ and look for a plane of symmetry through the substituted carbon and the opposite ring carbon to group equivalent $^{13}\text{C}$ atoms.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbons using symmetry**
Cyclohexylmethanol has 7 carbons total: 6 in the ring plus 1 in $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. The $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ carbon is unique. In the chair ring there is a mirror plane through C1 (attached to $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$) and C4 opposite. So C1 is unique, C2 pairs with C6, C3 pairs with C5, and C4 is unique. That gives $1 + 4 = 5$ distinct environments, so 5 peaks in the $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectrum.
